title: Managing organic matter turnover
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/03%3A_Amount_of_Organic_Matter_in_Soils/3.09%3A_The_Dynamics_of_Raising_and_Maintaining_Soil_Organic_Matter_Levels#Equilibrium Levels of Organic Matter > Increasing Organic Matter Versus Managing Organic Matter Turnover

definition.text: Organic matter decomposes in all soils, so good management continually supplies new organic matter to feed organisms and replace what is lost.

facts.text: Minimize soil disturbance to keep aggregates and the organic matter inside them.
Keep the surface covered with living plants or cover crops, or with residue mulch.
Use rotations with perennials, cover crops and extensive-rooted crops, and add composts, manures or other off-field organic materials.

sources.title: 3.9: The Dynamics of Raising and Maintaining Soil Organic Matter Levels - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Practices to improve soil health should grow healthy plants, suppress pests or increase beneficial organisms while reducing environmental impact.

facts.text: They group into minimizing disturbance, keeping soil covered, maximizing biodiversity, managing water, and maintaining pH and nutrients without excessive loss.
Organic matter practices come first for long-term sustainability, since each has multiple benefits; good physical condition and nutrient management need additional practices.

sources.title: 9.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Different crop residues and manures vary in chemistry, so they differ in how fast they decompose and in what they do for soil organic matter and aggregation.

facts.text: Residues low in hemicellulose, polyphenols and lignin, such as green legume cover crops and soybean residue, decompose fast and have a shorter effect on organic matter than cornstalks or wheat straw.
Manure with much bedding decomposes slowly and lasts longer in soil, and ruminant manure lasts longer than that of grain-fed chickens and hogs.
Easily decomposed residues, manures, cover crops and straw boost aggregation more than compost, which has already decomposed, though compost raises water-holding capacity.

A variety of residues is needed to feed diverse organisms, supply nutrients and promote aggregation; lignin-rich straw or sawdust builds organic matter but needs added nitrogen or the microbes run short and less becomes humus.
After decomposition only about 10-20% of a residue is converted to stable humus.

title: Crop residue removal for fuel
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/09%3A_Managing_for_High-Quality_Soils_and_Focusing_on_Organic_Matter_Management/9.02%3A_Organic_Matter_Management#Using Organic Materials > Crop Residues: Fuel Versus Soil Organic Matter

definition.text: Using crop residues as biofuel feedstock could starve soil of organic inputs that maintain its quality.

facts.text: Most aboveground corn residue must return to soil: an estimated 2-5 tons of corn residue are needed to keep favourable properties.

A long-term New York study found modest cornstalk removal caused limited extra deterioration under no-till, yet routine removal calls for caution, most of all on cash grain fields with conventional tillage and no manure or compost.
Hans Jenny argued in 1980 against indiscriminate conversion of biomass and organic wastes to fuels, because the humus capital deserves to be maintained.

contested_note: Residue use as fuel is weighed against its value for soil organic matter, with limited evidence on how much removal is tolerable.

title: Practices promoting water infiltration
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/09%3A_Managing_for_High-Quality_Soils_and_Focusing_on_Organic_Matter_Management/9.02%3A_Organic_Matter_Management#Effects of Residue Characteristics on Soil > Practices Promoting Water Infiltration And Retention

definition.text: Practices that raise infiltration cut runoff and erosion, refill root-zone pores and recharge groundwater.

facts.text: A University of Nebraska review of 89 studies found perennial grass or legume hay and cover crops gave the greatest gains in rainfall infiltration.
No-till raised infiltration only inconsistently, but did so when combined with surface residues and cover crops.

title: Crop-livestock integration and soil organic matter
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/09%3A_Managing_for_High-Quality_Soils_and_Focusing_on_Organic_Matter_Management/9.02%3A_Organic_Matter_Management#Organic Matter Management on Different Types of Farms

definition.text: Animal-based farms maintain soil organic matter more easily because manure recycles carbon and nutrients from farm-grown feed.

facts.text: Integrating crops and livestock can start an upward spiral: manure improves soil, crops produce more residue and feed, and more animals mean more manure.
Pasture, hay and haylage give an economic use for perennial forages in rotation, and manure can be obtained by trading hay with neighbours.

sources.title: 9.2: Organic Matter Management - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

definition.text: Organic matter practices bring nutrients and help manage them, but specific nutrient practices are still needed.

facts.text: A legume cover crop adds active organic matter, cuts erosion and supplies nitrogen to the next crop; cover and deep-rooted crops cycle nitrate, potassium, calcium and magnesium that might leach.
Importing manure or compost adds nutrients and can overload soil if applied routinely every year; testing manure, timing nutrients, liming and soil tests are separate practices.

title: Afforestation and soil carbon
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW CAN WE MANAGE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Land Management

definition.text: Deforestation typically lowers soil carbon, while afforestation may partly restore the original levels.

facts.text: Boreal reforestation gains carbon more slowly than other climates because trees grow slowly, and previous land use and disturbance type control the rate.
Afforested farmland gains more soil carbon than pasture or grassland, and mine-disturbed soils also gain a lot.
Where suited, deciduous trees raise soil carbon faster than conifers and over time store more in the mineral soil than in the forest floor.

sources.title: 1.3: Soil Organic Matter - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

title: Energetics of organic matter degradation
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#WHERE DOES SOIL ORGANIC MATTER COME FROM AND WHY DOES IT PERSIST? > Degradation of Carbon Inputs

definition.text: Under aerobic conditions microbes respire organic inputs to carbon dioxide and water, using oxygen as electron acceptor, and the rate depends on input chemistry.

facts.text: Cellulose breaks into simple sugars that are readily degraded, whereas lignin, a network of aromatic components, is hard to break down and mainly degraded by fungi.
More complex organic matter needs more chemical energy and oxygen to degrade, one reason it persists longer.
Fresh plant residue can fuel microbial activity that degrades stored carbon (priming), or it can add to stored carbon, depending on input quality, microbes, oxygen, water and time.
Respiration is much slower without oxygen, so conversion of plant carbon takes longer in anaerobic soils.

sources.title: 1.3: Soil Organic Matter - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

title: Mineral protection of organic matter
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#WHERE DOES SOIL ORGANIC MATTER COME FROM AND WHY DOES IT PERSIST? > Persistence of Soil Organic Matter

definition.text: Organic matter persists for decades to centuries largely because it binds to minerals and is physically protected inside aggregates.

facts.text: Clay minerals bind organic matter by covalent, ionic or van der Waals interactions, making it hard for microbes to reach.
Iron and aluminium oxides do this in acidic soils, and calcium and magnesium bridges link organic molecules to clay in neutral and alkaline soils.
2:1 clays with higher surface area adsorb more carbon than 1:1 clays.
Inside aggregates, organic matter is spatially separated from decomposers and has less oxygen.
Pyrogenic carbon from boreal fires, with condensed aromatic structures, can persist as a long-term sink, though persistence varies with formation conditions.

sources.title: 1.3: Soil Organic Matter - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

title: Rethinking soil organic matter
article: History of soil science#Soil organic matter

facts.text: Historically stability was blamed on humic substances formed from inputs and extracted with strong base and acid, interpreted as large stable macromolecules.
From the late 1990s high-resolution chemistry showed soil organic matter is recognizable plant and animal biomolecules at varying degradation stages that can associate like larger molecules.

A newer paradigm holds that molecular structure alone does not explain persistence; microbial carbon-use efficiency matters, and labile molecules taken up by microbes may form most stable organic matter.
Flaws in the established paradigm showed in 1999, when soil models could not account for the large charcoal component of Chernozems.

contested_note: The humification theory still appears in textbooks while some researchers argue it is wrong.

title: Dry combustion carbon analysis
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW DO WE MEASURE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Dry Combustion

definition.text: Dry combustion burns a ground soil sample in oxygen and measures the CO2 and nitrogen released to give total carbon and nitrogen together.

facts.text: Samples under 250 μm are burned at about 1250°C in oxygen; copper at 600°C reduces nitrogen oxides to N2, and a gas chromatograph separates CO2 from N2 for detection.
To get organic carbon, carbonates are removed by acid, measured by neutralization, or avoided by burning at 860°C, which decomposes only organic carbon.

title: Walkley-Black wet oxidation
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW DO WE MEASURE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Wet Oxidation

definition.text: The Walkley-Black method oxidizes organic carbon with chromate, heated by added sulfuric acid, and titrates leftover chromate to get carbon.

facts.text: It was once the standard method but oxidizes carbon incompletely, so a correction factor that varies with soil type is needed and biases results.
Carbon present as charcoal may be missed, underestimating total soil carbon.

sources.title: 1.3: Soil Organic Matter - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

title: Soil organic matter to carbon conversion
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW DO WE MEASURE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > Soil Organic Matter vs Soil Organic Carbon and the Conversion Issue

definition.text: Soil organic carbon and soil organic matter are different quantities, though they are routinely converted by assuming carbon is 58% of organic matter mass (factor 1.72).

facts.text: The 58% figure comes from Waksman and Stevens (1930), who urged caution; organic matter also holds hydrogen (about 4%) and oxygen (about 30%) that vary with decomposition state.
Reviews of many studies find actual factors are usually higher than 1.72, meaning carbon is a smaller share of organic matter.
The best approach is separate direct analyses; otherwise state what was analyzed and how values were converted.

sources.title: 1.3: Soil Organic Matter - Geosciences LibreTexts (Digging into Canadian Soils)

title: Carbonate interference in carbon analysis
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/01%3A_Digging_In/1.03%3A_Soil_Organic_Matter#HOW DO WE MEASURE SOIL ORGANIC MATTER? > The Carbonate Issue

definition.text: Carbonates in soil decompose to CO2 during combustion-based analysis, inflating the estimate of organic carbon.

facts.text: The problem arises on limestone-derived soils, including surface soils where tillage erosion has exposed carbonate-rich horizons.
Three approaches separate carbonate carbon from organic carbon: heat treatment, acid treatment and wet oxidation.

definition.text: A plant or plant-like organism that grows on the surface of another plant, taking moisture and nutrients from air, rain or accumulated debris.

facts.text: Epiphytes use the host (phorophyte) only for support and, unlike parasitic plants, draw no nourishment from it; they are not rooted in soil.
Without soil they depend on fog, dew, rain, mist, nutrients leached or decomposed from rooted plants, and nitrogen fixation.
Holo-epiphytes never touch the ground, like orchids; hemi-epiphytes such as strangler figs spend only part of life off the ground.
Epiphytes hold water in the canopy, reducing water input to the soil, and cool and moisten the host canopy, which may cut its transpiration.
